html:
The Ainu are the native people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and once of northern Honshu. The map uses their name for the far north of Japan all the way from 3000 BCE, standing for the people of that land long before written records.

Their roots go back to the hunters and fishers of Jōmon Japan. When rice farming and the Yayoi way of life spread through southern Japan in the first millennium BCE, the north kept its older ways. In Hokkaido the Satsumon culture, and on the northern coasts the seal-hunting Okhotsk culture, came before the Ainu culture that took shape around the 1200s.

Ainu life rested on salmon fishing, deer hunting, gathering and trade. They had no writing; their history lived in long spoken epics, the yukar. Bears held a special place, and the bear-sending ceremony, iomante, returned a raised bear's spirit to the gods.

Trade bound them to Japan and the mainland: furs, fish and eagle feathers went south for iron, rice, lacquerware and sake. From the 1600s the Matsumae domain controlled that trade on harsh terms. The Ainu rose against it in Shakushain's revolt of 1669 and lost. After the Meiji Restoration Japan annexed Hokkaido in 1869, settled it with farmers and pressed the Ainu to give up their language and customs. Japan recognized them in law as an indigenous people only in 2019.
